title: Imperative
goal: By the end of this lesson you can give instructions, advice and encouragement with the imperative (tu, nous and vous forms), make negative commands, and understand Quebec favourites like Envoye! and Lâche pas!

body: The imperative is for orders, instructions and suggestions. It has only three forms (tu, nous, vous) and you drop the subject pronoun: *Tu manges.* → *Mange!* *Vous écoutez.* → *Écoutez!*
The *nous* form means 'let's': *Allons au parc!* (Let's go to the park!)
Key rule: -er verbs (and *aller*) lose the *s* in the *tu* form: *tu parles → Parle!*, *tu vas → Va!* Other verbs keep it: *tu finis → Finis!*, *tu prends → Prends!*
learn.tip: -er verbs: no s in the tu command. Mange! Écoute! Va!

learn.h: The irregular ones: être, avoir, savoir
body: Three common verbs have special imperative forms. You'll mostly see them in set phrases: *Sois sage!* (Be good!), *Soyez prudents!* (Be careful!), *N'aie pas peur!* (Don't be afraid!)
For a negative command, put *ne … pas* around the verb: *Ne parle pas!* *Ne mangez pas ça!* *N'oublie pas!*

Reflexive verbs put the pronoun AFTER the verb with a hyphen in the affirmative; *te* becomes *toi*: *Lève-toi!* *Dépêchez-vous!* *Asseyons-nous.* In the negative, the pronoun goes back before the verb: *Ne te lève pas!* *Ne vous inquiétez pas.*
learn.tip: Affirmative: verb-toi. Negative: ne te verb pas.

body: A bare imperative can sound abrupt with strangers. Add *s'il te plaît / s'il vous plaît*: *Fermez la porte, s'il vous plaît.*
A question is even softer: *Tu peux fermer la porte?* *Pouvez-vous répéter?* On signs and forms you'll see the formal *Veuillez* + infinitive: *Veuillez patienter.* (Please wait.)
*Envoye!* (from *envoyer*, often said 'enweille') is the all-purpose Quebec push: Go on! Come on! Hurry up! Do it! *Envoye, on part!*

*Lâche pas!* means 'Don't give up! Hang in there!' — the most encouraging thing you'll hear. Notice the *ne* is dropped, as usual in speech. Other everyday ones: *Arrête donc!* (Come on, stop it! / No way!), *Voyons donc!* (Come on now!), *Fais attention!*

examples.fr: Va au dépanneur, s'il te plaît.
examples.en: Go to the corner store, please.
Let's go to the movies tonight!

examples.fr: Fermez la porte, s'il vous plaît.

examples.note: negative reflexive: pronoun before the verb
formal, on signs and phone lines

examples.fr: Envoye, on va être en retard!
examples.en: Come on, we're going to be late!
Don't give up, you can do it!

quebec.intro: Quebec has two imperatives you'll hear daily: 'Envoye!' to push someone to go or act, and 'Lâche pas!' to encourage them. Both drop the 'ne' and both are friendly and informal.

items.en: Don't give up! Hang in there!

items.note: donc softens or adds emphasis; also expresses surprise

drills.why: -er verbs drop the s in the tu imperative.
The nous form means let's. (On mange! also works in speech, but it isn't the imperative.)
In the negative, the pronoun returns before the verb.

a: Ferme la porte, s'il te plaît.
Fermez la porte, s'il vous plaît.

drills.why: Negative reflexive: ne + pronoun + verb + pas. In speech, ne drops (and Quebecers often say Inquiète-toi pas).

vocab.en: to be careful, to pay attention

vocab.fr: s'il te plaît / s'il vous plaît

pron.tip: LÂSH-pâ, with the long, back Quebec â.

dialogue.fr: Envoye, mets tes patins! Le match commence!
dialogue.en: Come on, put on your skates! The game is starting!

dialogue.fr: J'ai peur, papa. Les autres joueurs sont grands.
dialogue.en: I'm scared, Dad. The other players are big.

dialogue.fr: N'aie pas peur. Écoute ton coach et amuse-toi!
dialogue.en: Don't be afraid. Listen to your coach and have fun!
Get back up and keep going. Don't give up!

dialogue.fr: Promis. Allez, va! Et fais attention à la rondelle!
dialogue.en: Promise. Go on, go! And watch the puck!

questions.q: What should B do after falling?

speak.prompt: Give a friend three instructions to get to your place (go, take, turn…).
speak.model: Prends le métro jusqu'à Jean-Talon. Sors à droite. Marche deux minutes et sonne au 4520.

speak.prompt: Give two negative commands to a child.
speak.model: Ne mange pas de bonbons avant le souper! Ne te couche pas trop tard!

speak.prompt: Encourage a friend before an exam, Quebec style.
speak.model: Lâche pas! T'es capable! Envoye, tu vas réussir!

write.prompt: Write 6 tips for a newcomer surviving their first Quebec winter, using the imperative (tu or vous).
write.model: Achetez une bonne tuque et des mitaines. Habillez-vous chaudement. Ne sortez pas sans vos bottes. Faites attention à la glace sur les trottoirs. Allez patiner au parc, c'est le fun! Et surtout, lâchez pas: le printemps arrive!

quiz.q: How many imperative forms are there?

quiz.why: Only -er verbs and aller drop the s.

quiz.q: In 'Lève-toi', why toi and not te?
options: Te becomes toi after the verb in affirmative commands
quiz.why: Affirmative commands use the stressed pronoun after the verb.
Veuillez + infinitive is formal written politeness.

options: push someone to go or act

quiz.q: Which is the most polite way to ask a stranger?
quiz.why: A question with pouvez-vous and s'il vous plaît is softest.
